conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that regular intake of vitamin C does not prevent colds in the general population, citing Cochrane reviews and other evidence showing no effect on cold incidence, despite minor benefits for duration or specific high-stress exceptions.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**Conclusion: No — regular intake of vitamin C does not prevent colds for most people.**

The evidence consistently shows that routine vitamin C supplementation does not reduce the incidence of colds in the general population. The Cochrane review (29 trial comparisons, 11,306 participants) found that "regular ingestion of vitamin C had no effect on common cold incidence in the ordinary population" [1]. InformedHealth.org similarly states that "taking vitamin C every day to try to prevent colds won't protect most people from colds" [2]. WebMD concludes experts have found "little to no benefit from vitamin C for preventing or treating the common cold" [3].

**What vitamin C does do:** Regular supplementation (≥0.2 g/day) modestly shortens cold duration — by about 8% in adults and 14% in children — and may reduce severity by roughly 15% [1][4]. Starting vitamin C after symptoms begin has no effect [2].

**One exception:** In people under short periods of extreme physical stress (e.g., marathon runners, skiers), vitamin C halved cold risk in five trials [1]. This does not apply to the general population.

The popular belief that vitamin C prevents colds traces largely to Linus Pauling's 1970 book, which subsequent large-scale trials have not supported [1].

**Sources:**
[1] https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD000980_vitamin-c-preventing-and-treating-common-cold
[2] https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK279544/
[3] https://www.webmd.com/cold-and-flu/vitamin-c-for-common-cold
[4] https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12889-023-17229-8
